units.load1_at_launch: 1-minute load average of Linux at the launch of the process
units.gap_s: seconds between the end of the previous 120-thread process of the rerun and this launch (1 s resolution). bwx12 records: the launch of their process. units.passes: part A only: total_bytes / bytes_per_thread of the interval row. For read, asmread, write and asmwrite this is the number of buffer passes of all threads in the interval. units.min_ms: shortest length of one interval, milliseconds
units.speed_MTps: memory speed, million transfers per second

rate_kinds.part_A: aggregate_GBps column of the csv (sum of bytes / longest per-thread time)

verdicts.q1: Yes. At 7200 MT/s with 12 memory modules the new read kernel is still below the old read kernel. Part C (bwx12 kernel read against oldread of the same process and round, common stop, 6 s): 30.5 % to 31.2 % lower when read ran directly after oldread (4 pairs, 2 processes: T72C1, T72C3), and 29.7 % to 31.1 % lower when read ran directly after asmread (4 pairs, 2 processes: T72C2, T72C4). Part L, asmread (the same loop, used in place of the new read kernel) against oldread: 29.2 % to 30.5 % lower (6 pairs, 3 processes, 3 sessions). Part A, the repeat of the 2026-11-13 test, bw_new read against bw_old read, whole-pass stop, 0.5 s: 28.5 % to 31.8 % lower (6 pairs of process medians, 3 sessions). The percent values of part A are less exact than those of parts L and C. The new read kernel is below the old read kernel in all 8 pairs of part C and in all 6 pairs of part A. asmread is below the old read kernel in all 6 pairs of part L and in all 8 pairs of part C (30.8 % to 31.2 % after read, 30.1 % to 31.7 % as first interval, 29.7 % to 30.6 % after oldread). The size is not one fixed value: control I (idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) gave 31.9 % to 32.8 %, and the earlier run F72d12 of the same boot (not part of the rerun) gave 35.4 %. All values come from 1 boot.
verdicts.q2: Old read kernel. Part A (bw_old read): "no difference seen" (7200 MT/s: 459.90 to 474.15 GB/s, n = 18 intervals / 6 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot. 8000 MT/s: 463.58 to 469.03 GB/s, n = 21 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). The test cannot exclude a difference of about 1.2 % (est. from one boot), which is the width of the 8000 MT/s range. Part C (oldread): "no difference seen" (7200 MT/s: 464.00 to 468.14 GB/s, n = 8 intervals / 4 processes / 3 sessions and 1 extra process / 1 boot. 8000 MT/s: 465.53 to 470.05 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). There the test cannot exclude a difference of about 1.0 % (est. from one boot). This comparison of part C with 8000 MT/s follows rules V1 point 2, V2 point 4 and V4. Rule F2 points 2 and 3 would present part C at 7200 MT/s only (decision (r) in section 2). Part L (oldread): "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" (7200 MT/s: 461.61 to 464.29 GB/s, n = 6 intervals / 3 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot. 8000 MT/s: 465.53 to 470.05 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). Part L is lower by 1.24 GB/s at the nearest ends (0.3 % of the lower end of the 8000 MT/s range, 465.53 GB/s) and by 6.27 GB/s between the medians (1.3 % of the 8000 MT/s median, 468.91 GB/s). Two other rows of the same line in the same 7200 MT/s boot overlap the 8000 MT/s range. F72d12 (1 process at 20:02 UTC, before the rerun, load 0.34 at launch) gave 467.46 to 468.44 GB/s. Control I (2 processes, idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) gave 466.30 to 469.20 GB/s. So against the whole pool L-1 to L-4, only the range of part L, which started 5 s after part A, lies below the 8000 MT/s range among the bwx12 runs. A view added after the numbers were seen splits the 8000 MT/s pool by start state: the 5 bwx12 processes of the pool that started 5 s to 25 s after a 120-thread bwx12 process gave 468.56 to 470.05 GB/s (7 intervals / 5 processes / 1 boot), the highest oldread values of the pool. Part L is 4.27 GB/s below them. Part C started 5 s after 120-thread work too. It is 0.42 GB/s below them at the nearest ends, and its 4 position-matched intervals (cfwd, position 0) are 0.73 GB/s below them. Limit: these 5 processes are not all 8000 MT/s processes with that kind of start state. Against the other-binary processes that started after 120-thread work, part C overlaps (bwx11: 467.86 to 469.96 GB/s, 4 intervals / 3 processes. Runner bwx, position 0: 467.34 to 472.95 GB/s, 48 intervals / 24 processes). Part L lies below every oldread interval at 8000 MT/s with 12 modules that this sheet holds (the lowest is 465.53 GB/s, row L-2, process p1nop). So the 8000 MT/s rows do not show that a start after 120-thread work lowers the old read kernel. The data do not show that the boot or the memory speed is the cause: each memory speed has one boot. Insufficient data: why part L was lower. The like.spec line, run in turn from an idle start and directly after part A, at least 3 times each, in one boot, would resolve it (the measurement of hypothesis H1 in section 6). New read kernel. Part A (bw_new read, session 1): outside the 8000 MT/s range of the same round in both rounds. Round 1: 32.75 to 35.91 GB/s above the upper end of the round-1 range (297.34 GB/s). Round 2: 10.37 to 16.51 GB/s above the upper end of the round-2 range (316.31 GB/s). n per round at 7200 MT/s: 3 intervals / 1 process / session 1 / 1 boot. n per round at 8000 MT/s: 6 intervals / 2 processes / 1 boot. The pass counts differ, so part A gives no exact size. Part L (asmread, the same loop, used in place of the new read kernel): "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" (7200 MT/s: 321.65 to 327.93 GB/s, n = 6 intervals / 3 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot. 8000 MT/s: 288.54 to 309.17 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). Part C, asmread directly after oldread (crev, round 1, position 0): "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" (7200 MT/s: 324.73 to 326.12 GB/s, n = 2 intervals / 2 processes / session 2 and 1 extra process / 1 boot. 8000 MT/s: 288.54 to 309.17 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). Part C is higher by 15.56 GB/s at the nearest ends. This baseline matches in the kernel that ran directly before. It does not match in the position: asmread is at position 1 in rows L-1 to L-4. This comparison of part C with 8000 MT/s follows rules V1 point 2, V2 point 4 and V4. Rule F2 points 2 and 3 would present part C at 7200 MT/s only (decision (r) in section 2). Two corrected hardware error records fall inside the 8000 MT/s interval with the lowest asmread value (288.54 GB/s). Without this interval the 8000 MT/s range is 298.61 to 309.17 GB/s (10 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot), and no wording changes (sections 4.1 and 4.4). Part C (kernel read): Insufficient data: no 8000 MT/s run of kernel read with bwx12. The same line in the same 7200 MT/s boot gave asmread 301.90 to 302.78 GB/s at 20:02 UTC (F72d12, before the rerun, n = 2 intervals / 1 process / no session / 1 boot). That is inside the range of the 8000 MT/s pool L-1 to L-4. Against L-1 alone it is 1.73 GB/s higher. F72d12 is an idle start only by the load-average rule of this sheet: its process list, written 5 s before the launch, shows pr/ttyAMA-1 at 51.6 %CPU (section 4.6). Control I (idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) gave asmread 313.78 to 317.60 GB/s (n = 4 intervals / 2 processes / no session / 1 boot). That is also above every bwx12 row of the fixed 8000 MT/s list, by 4.61 GB/s at the nearest ends (13.62 GB/s against L-1 alone). The three visits of the boot span 301.90 to 327.93 GB/s. Inside this one boot at one memory speed, part L lies 18.87 GB/s above F72d12 at the nearest ends and 20.54 GB/s between the medians. That is more than the distance of part L to the 8000 MT/s range (12.48 GB/s at the nearest ends, 17.61 GB/s between the medians). Between the farthest ends the order is the opposite (26.03 GB/s inside the boot against 39.38 GB/s to the 8000 MT/s range). Insufficient data: whether a difference of the new read kernel comes from the memory speed. Speed and boot changed together. Two boots at equal settings (10 modules, one process each) gave asmread 260.37 / 262.67 and 285.57 / 286.45 GB/s, 9.4 % apart (medians). Runs in several boots per speed would resolve it (needs reboots, not part of this task).

insufficient_data: Insufficient data: whether a difference of the new read kernel comes from the memory speed. Speed and boot changed together. Two boots at equal settings (10 modules, one process each) gave asmread 260.37 / 262.67 and 285.57 / 286.45 GB/s, 9.4 % apart (medians). Runs in several boots per speed would resolve it (needs reboots, not part of this task).
Insufficient data: why the load-only loop differs between the three visits of the same boot (section 4.6). The measurements named under H1 and H2 would resolve it.

Insufficient data: why old read was 461.61 to 464.29 GB/s in part L and 466.30 to 469.20 GB/s in control I (added after the first numbers were seen). The 8000 MT/s rows do not point to the start state: there the 5 bwx12 processes that started after 120-thread work gave higher oldread values (468.56 to 470.05 GB/s, 7 intervals / 5 processes) than the 2 processes that started at a load below 1.0 (465.53 to 468.06 GB/s, 4 intervals / 2 processes) (section 4.2, view added after the numbers were seen). The measurement named under H1 would resolve it.

Insufficient data: no 8000 MT/s run of kernel read with bwx12. A run of cfwd.spec and crev.spec at 8000 MT/s would resolve it (needs a change of the firmware setting and a reboot, so root and approval).
Insufficient data: whether hardware error records occurred during the rerun. A count of the "[Hardware Error]" lines of the kernel log would resolve it (needs root).
Insufficient data: a direct reading of the memory speed during the rerun. `sudo dmidecode -t 17` would resolve it (needs root). The proof used here is the equal boot id.
Insufficient data: whether the one-thread phase of 2026-11-13 changes the 120-thread rates (section 1.5).
Insufficient data: whether the buffers of part A lay on 2 MiB pages. bandwidth.c does not record it. A run of the same kernels with bwx12 records it in "P" rows.

Insufficient data: the applied memory speed in the boot of the 8000 MT/s baselines. That boot is over, so the reading cannot be taken any more. The firmware setting of that boot is on record (section 1.5, point 10).

Insufficient data: the firmware settings in the boot of the rerun, apart from the memory speed. The two TXREQ settings were set back before the 7200 MT/s reboot test, and the settings list saved after that is equal to the list of the baseline boot in its 604 readable values. No list was saved in the boot of the rerun. A settings list saved in that boot would resolve it (needs root) (section 1.5, point 13).

Insufficient data: whether a corrected hardware error record lowers the rate of an interval (hypothesis in section 4.1). The processes of rows L-1 to L-4, R0 and R0b hold 8 intervals to which records can be assigned (all kernels and positions, view added after the numbers were seen). 3 of them are more than 1 GB/s below the same kernel at the same position in the other round of their process (1.96, 3.69 and 10.07 GB/s). The other 5 differ from it by less than 1 GB/s (-0.04 to +0.70 GB/s). Without records the two rounds of the same processes differ by up to 6.24 GB/s. This comparison is not a test. A run that stores the kernel log time of every record beside the interval times would resolve it (needs root).
hypotheses: H1, start state. The rate of the load-only loop depends on the work that ran shortly before the launch. What fits: part L (launched 5 s after part A) gave 321.65 to 327.93 GB/s, and control I (idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) gave 313.78 to 317.60 GB/s. In part A the second round is above the first in 8 of 9 load-only cells. What does not fit: at 8000 MT/s process p2 of row R0 (other binary bwx11, load 85.15 at launch) gave 296.02 to 296.22 GB/s, below p1 (load 0.00) with 302.59 to 303.16 GB/s. The bwx12 rows of the fixed list do not fit either (section 4.2, view by start state): the 5 processes that started 5 s to 25 s after a 120-thread bwx12 process (L-2 p2add, L-3 thp, L-4 st1, L-4 st2, L-4 st3, load 53.98 to 94.23) gave asmread 288.54 to 309.17 GB/s (7 intervals / 5 processes), and the 2 processes that started at a load below 1.0 (L-1 a6456, L-2 p1nop) gave 298.71 to 305.57 GB/s (4 intervals / 2 processes). The two ranges overlap. Inside row L-2, p2add (load 94.23) gave 298.61 and 288.54 GB/s, below p1nop (load 0.00) with 305.57 and 302.90 GB/s. For oldread the order is the opposite at 8000 MT/s: the same 5 processes gave 468.56 to 470.05 GB/s, above the 465.53 to 468.06 GB/s of the 2 processes at a load below 1.0. At 7200 MT/s oldread of part L (461.61 to 464.29 GB/s) was below control I (466.30 to 469.20 GB/s). Also, in part A the first-round process of bw_new read gave 330.09 to 333.25 GB/s in session 1 (idle start), above session 2 (322.67 to 325.26 GB/s) and session 3 (315.55 to 320.89 GB/s), which started 5 s after 120-thread work. Measurement that would confirm or reject it: the like.spec line, alternating between an idle start and a start directly after part A, at least 3 times each, in one boot.

H2, time since boot. The rate of the load-only loop rises with the time since boot or with the work done since boot. What fits: F72d12 ran 20 s after the first kernel log line of the boot and gave the lowest values. The first process of the rerun started 2 h 9 min 58 s after that line. Limit: F72d12 also differs from control I (added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) in its process list (pr/ttyAMA-1 at 51.6 %CPU, 5 s before the launch, section 4.6). So the time since boot and the start phase of the machine are not separated. Measurement: repeat the idle-start line of control I some hours later in the same boot, and once directly after a reboot (a reboot needs approval).

H3, memory speed. 7200 MT/s raises the rate of the load-only loop. The rerun cannot separate this from H1, H2 and the boot. Measurement: the like.spec line in several boots per speed (needs reboots and a change of the firmware setting).

H4, pass counts in part A. An interval with 664 passes has 6 passes on the 64 threads of mesh 0 and 5 passes on the 56 threads of mesh 1 (64 x 6 + 56 x 5 = 664). threads120.csv has no row per thread, so the split is not proven. Measurement: part A with the option --per-thread.
H5, load values. The high load values at the launches come from the rerun's own earlier processes (section 1.3).

sentences: Q1: yes, at 7200 MT/s with 12 memory modules the new read kernel was still below the old read kernel: 30.5 % to 31.2 % lower when it ran directly after the old read kernel and 29.7 % to 31.1 % lower when it ran directly after asmread (part C, 6 s runs, 4 pairs each).

Q2, old read kernel: by the rule fixed before the run the result against the 8000 MT/s runs is "no difference seen" in the repeat of the 2026-11-13 test (part A, where the test cannot exclude a difference of about 1.2 %, est.) and in part C (about 1.0 %, est.), and the rate was lower in part L (461.61 to 464.29 GB/s, n = 6 intervals / 3 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot, against 465.53 to 470.05 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot), but the data do not show that the boot or the memory speed is the cause.

Q2, new read kernel: asmread (the hand-written loop with the same loads, used in place of the new read kernel) ran above every bwx12 row of the fixed 8000 MT/s list in part L (321.65 to 327.93 GB/s, n = 6 intervals / 3 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot, against 288.54 to 309.17 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot), in control I (313.78 to 317.60 GB/s, n = 4 intervals / 2 processes / no session / 1 boot, added after the first numbers were seen) and in the 2 part C intervals that ran directly after the old read kernel (324.73 to 326.12 GB/s), but an earlier run of the same line in the same 7200 MT/s boot gave 301.90 to 302.78 GB/s (F72d12, n = 2 intervals / 1 process / no session / 1 boot), and each memory speed has one boot, so the data do not show an effect of the memory speed.
detail: Q1, part L (6 s runs): asmread was 29.2 % to 30.5 % below the old read kernel (6 pairs).

Q1, part A (the repeat of the 2026-11-13 test, whole-pass stop, 0.5 s): the new read kernel was 28.5 % to 31.8 % below the old read kernel (6 pairs of process medians). These percent values are less exact than those of parts L and C (section 3.1).

Q2, old read kernel, the two comparisons with the wording "no difference seen": part A gave 459.90 to 474.15 GB/s (n = 18 intervals / 6 processes / 3 sessions / 1 boot) against 463.58 to 469.03 GB/s (n = 21 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). Part C gave 464.00 to 468.14 GB/s (n = 8 intervals / 4 processes / 3 sessions and 1 extra process / 1 boot) against 465.53 to 470.05 GB/s (n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). The size that the test cannot exclude is the width of the 8000 MT/s range: 1.2 % of its lower end in part A and 1.0 % in part C (est. from one boot). In part A the 7200 MT/s range is wider than the 8000 MT/s range (14.25 GB/s against 5.45 GB/s): 3 of its 18 intervals lie below that range and 3 lie above it (section 4.2).

Q2, part C: the fixed rules contradict each other here. Rule F2 points 2 and 3 would present part C at 7200 MT/s only. This sheet follows rules V1 point 2, V2 point 4 and V4 and compares part C with the 8000 MT/s rows (decision (r) in section 2).

Q2, old read kernel: two other rows of the same line in the same 7200 MT/s boot lie inside the range of the 8000 MT/s pool L-1 to L-4. F72d12 (1 process at 20:02 UTC, before the rerun) gave 467.46 to 468.44 GB/s. Control I (2 processes, idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) gave 466.30 to 469.20 GB/s.

Q2, old read kernel, view added after the numbers were seen (section 4.2): the 5 bwx12 processes of the pool L-1 to L-4 that started 5 s to 25 s after a 120-thread bwx12 process gave 468.56 to 470.05 GB/s (7 intervals / 5 processes / 1 boot). Part L and part C also started after 120-thread work. Both lie below these 5 processes: part L by 4.27 GB/s and part C by 0.42 GB/s at the nearest ends. Limit: these 5 processes are not all 8000 MT/s processes with that kind of start state. Against the other-binary processes that started after 120-thread work, part C overlaps (bwx11: 467.86 to 469.96 GB/s, 4 intervals / 3 processes. Runner bwx, position 0: 467.34 to 472.95 GB/s, 48 intervals / 24 processes). Part L lies below these rows too.

Q2, old read kernel: Insufficient data: why part L was lower. The like.spec line, run in turn from an idle start and directly after part A, at least 3 times each, in one boot, would resolve it (the measurement of hypothesis H1 in section 6).

Q2, new read kernel, asmread in the three visits of the 7200 MT/s boot: F72d12 lies inside the range of the 8000 MT/s pool L-1 to L-4. Against L-1 alone (the baseline row with the identical argument line) it is 1.73 GB/s higher. F72d12 is an idle start only by the load-average rule of this sheet: its process list, written 5 s before the launch, shows pr/ttyAMA-1 at 51.6 %CPU (section 4.6). Control I (idle start, added after the first numbers were seen, not part of the plan fixed before the run) lies above every bwx12 row of the fixed 8000 MT/s list, by 4.61 GB/s at the nearest ends (13.62 GB/s against L-1 alone). The three visits (F72d12, part L, control I) span 301.90 to 327.93 GB/s.

Q2, new read kernel, part C: asmread directly after oldread (crev, round 1, position 0) gave 324.73 to 326.12 GB/s (n = 2 intervals / 2 processes / session 2 and 1 extra process / 1 boot). By rule V1 point 2 the wording is "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" against the pool L-1 to L-4 (288.54 to 309.17 GB/s, n = 11 intervals / 7 processes / 1 boot). Part C is higher by 15.56 GB/s at the nearest ends. The baseline matches in the kernel that ran directly before. It does not match in the position: asmread is at position 1 in rows L-1 to L-4. This comparison follows decision (r) in section 2.
Q2, new read kernel: the new read kernel itself (bw_new read) lies outside (above) the 8000 MT/s range of the same round in session 1 of part A. The bwx12 kernel read has no 8000 MT/s run.

Q2, machine state: the hardware error records during the rerun are not known (the kernel log was not read). At 8000 MT/s, 2 corrected records fall inside the interval with the lowest asmread value of the pool L-1 to L-4 (288.54 GB/s). Without this interval the pool spans 298.61 to 309.17 GB/s, and no wording changes (sections 4.1 and 4.4). The firmware settings of the boot of the rerun were not read, apart from the memory speed (section 1.5, point 13).
Q2, new read kernel: Insufficient data: whether a difference comes from the memory speed. Runs in several boots per speed would resolve it.
